sib.t: Generative AI and the Nature of Work

dom.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment

st.t: AI infrastructure: Scale advantages need not create monopoly
st.an: The source establishes the technical premise that model quality depends strongly on compute, parameters and dataset size, and documents rising resource commitments. However, it does not assess whether these scale advantages cause market concentration, monopoly or durable infrastructure control, so its position on the cluster’s principal proposition cannot be determined.
qs: Recent progress in generative AI has been driven by four factors: computing scale, earlier innovations in model architecture, the ability to “pre-train” using large amounts of unlabeled data and refinements in training techniques.8         First, the quality of LLMs is strongly dependent on scale: the amount of computing power used for training, the number of model parameters, and dataset size (Kaplan et al., 2020).

st.an: The supplied excerpt is only a bibliography and states no findings or arguments about benchmark quality, reproducibility, governance, or the relationship between benchmark scores and workplace performance. The cited titles alone do not establish the source’s position relative to the cluster proposition.

st.t: Professional evaluation: Realistic tasks complicate reproducible scoring
st.an: The supplied source excerpt is bibliography only and provides no substantive claims, findings, or recommendations about evaluating professional task execution, reproducible scoring, automated judging, or self-correction. Its position relative to the cluster proposition therefore cannot be determined.

st.t: Generative automation: Fluent work product still needs authority
st.an: The source accepts that generative AI expands the tasks machines can perform while remaining unreliable in broader, high-stakes real-world settings. It materially extends the cluster by proposing tacit-knowledge transfer as a mechanism for augmentation or substitution and by emphasizing workers’ ability to identify when AI assistance is ineffective.
qs: Generative AI tools can not only expand the types of tasks that machines can perform, they may also reveal valuable information about how the most productive human workers differ from others.

This raises concerns both about whether AI tools will be able to provide accurate assistance in every circumstance and— perhaps more importantly—about whether workers will be able to distinguish cases where AI tools are effective from those where they are not.

st.t: Aggregate productivity: Task speedups shrink during scaling
st.an: The source supports the synthesis’s distinction between task-level gains and broader labour-market conclusions. It finds substantial productivity gains concentrated among initially lower-skilled workers, with no gain for the most skilled, but does not establish effects on aggregate productivity, wages, inequality or entry-level employment.
qs: In Panel A, we show that the productivity impact of AI assistance is most pronounced for workers in the lowest skill quintile (leftmost side), who see a .29 log point or 34% increase in resolutions per hour.
In contrast, AI assistance does not lead to any productivity increase for the most skilled workers (rightmost side).

st.t: Assisted inequality: Productivity gains need not improve careers
st.an: The study directly supports the cluster’s distinction between assisted task performance and career outcomes: it finds substantial workplace productivity gains, concentrated among lower-skilled and newer agents, while explicitly stating that its data cannot establish effects on wages, labour demand or hiring composition. Its suggestive learning evidence and cautions about generalisation also align with the cluster’s outcome-specific framing.
qs: We find that access to AI assistance increases the productivity of agents by 14%, as measured by the number of customer issues they are able to resolve per hour.
Unfortunately, our data do not allow us to observe changes in wages, overall labor demand, or the skill composition of workers hired for the job.

st.t: Assisted performance: Gains vary by skill measure
st.an: The source directly supports the cluster’s distinction among performance dimensions: AI deployment significantly reduced handling time and increased throughput, but produced only weak evidence of better resolution rates and no statistically significant customer-satisfaction improvement. It therefore shows task-specific gains rather than uniform performance improvement.
qs: Post AI X Treated measures the impact of AI model deployment after deployment on treated agents for average handle time or average      call duration, chats per hour, the number of chats an agent handles per hour, resolution rate, the share of technical support problems they can resolve and net      promoter score (NPS), an estimate of customer satisfaction, and each metrics corresponding natural log equivalents.

st.t: Knowledge work: Task gains do not ensure skill growth
st.an: The study directly supports the cluster’s separation of assisted task performance from durable learning and broader labour-market effects. It finds substantial but uneven workplace productivity gains, offers only suggestive evidence of learning during outages, and explicitly does not establish longer-term effects on skills, job design, wages or demand.
qs: Access to the tool increases productivity, as measured by issues resolved per hour, by 14% on average, including a 34% improvement for novice and low-skilled workers but with minimal impact on experienced and highly skilled workers.
Most importantly, our results do not capture the potential longer-term impacts of generative AI on skill demand, job design, wages, or customer demand.

st.t: Legal workflows: Immediate gains create competence risks
st.an: Although based on customer support rather than legal practice, the workplace evidence supports the cluster’s core augmentation framing: AI produced substantial but uneven productivity gains while humans retained responsibility. It also reinforces the importance of user capability, reliability limits and organisational complements, and does not infer worker displacement from productivity gains.
qs: It is designed to augment agents, who remain responsible for the conversation and are free to ignore its suggestions.
Promising technologies may have more limited effects in practice due to the need for complementary organizational investments, skill development, or business process redesign.

st.t: Productivity distribution: Weaker users do not always gain most
st.an: The source supports the cluster’s conditional account: in this customer-support workflow, gains were concentrated among novice and lower-skilled workers, while experienced and highly skilled workers benefited little. It also cautions that practical effects depend on workers’ ability to judge AI reliability and on complementary skills, organizational investment and process redesign, rather than access alone.
qs: Access to the tool increases productivity, as measured by issues resolved per hour, by 14% on average, including a 34% improvement for novice and low-skilled workers but with minimal impact on experienced and highly skilled workers.
Promising technologies may have more limited effects in practice due to the need for complementary organizational investments, skill development, or business process redesign.

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: The source directly supports selective, human-controlled augmentation: it finds substantial productivity gains in a bounded workplace task, strongly heterogeneous effects by worker skill, and unresolved reliability and generalisability. It also reinforces the synthesis’s emphasis on user judgment, skill development and complementary process redesign rather than inferring autonomous competence or broad labour-market effects.

kp.k: Workplace evidence concerns customer support, not legal practice
kp.d: The supplied working-paper text studies a Fortune 500 enterprise software company's technical support agents, including outsourced workers, rather than lawyers. It observes 3 million chats by 5,179 agents, including 1,636 agents observed after AI deployment; 89% of agents were outside the United States, primarily in the Philippines. The bulk of adoption occurred between November 2020 and February 2021. These are cross-domain findings, not direct evidence about legal services.
qs: In total, we observe the conversation text and outcomes associated with 3 million chats by 5,179 agents.
The bulk of the adoption occurs between November 2020 and February 2021.
Most agents in our sample, 89%, are located outside of the United States, primarily in the Philippines.

kp.k: AI augments workers who retain responsibility and discretion
kp.d: The GPT-based system was fine-tuned on customer-service conversations labeled with outcomes and worker performance. It supplies real-time response suggestions and links to internal technical documentation. Suggestions are visible only to human agents, who can reject or modify them; the system withholds suggestions where training data are insufficient. The intervention therefore tests supervised assistance rather than autonomous customer-service substitution.
qs: Importantly, the AI system we study is designed to augment, rather than replace, human agents.
The output is shown only to the agent, who has full discretion over whether to incorporate (fully or partially) the AI suggestions.
Furthermore, the system does not provide suggestions when it has insufficient training data for that situation.

kp.k: Staggered deployment supports a qualified causal analysis
kp.d: The main analysis uses difference-in-differences with calendar-time, agent and tenure controls, rather than a large randomized experiment. Deployment followed a seven-week randomized pilot involving 50 agents, which was included but not analyzed separately. Event studies and alternative estimators address heterogeneous treatment effects, subject to identification assumptions. Resolution rates and customer satisfaction were available only for a subset of agents, limiting coverage of the principal productivity measure.
qs: We isolate the causal impact of access to AI recommendations using a standard difference-in- differences regression:
In our preferred specification, we also include controls for time-invariant agent-level fixed effects αi and time-varying agent tenure.
This, in turn, means that we only observe our omnibus productivity measure—resolutions per hour—for this smaller subset.

kp.k: Average productivity rises without average quality deterioration
kp.d: The authors report approximately 14% higher issues resolved per hour; the preferred level specification estimates 0.30 additional resolutions per hour, or 13.8%. Average chat duration falls 3.8 minutes, approximately 9%, and chats handled per hour increase roughly 14%, suggesting both faster handling and improved multitasking. Resolution rates rise 1.3 percentage points, significant at the 10% level, while surveyed customer satisfaction shows no economically significant change. Effects appear immediately and persist over the observed post-deployment period.
qs: with agent and tenure fixed effects, we find that the deployment of AI increases RPH by 0.30 chats or 13.8%.
This effect grows slightly in the second month and remains stable and persistent up to the end of our sample.
We therefore interpret these findings as saying that, on average, AI assistance increases productivity without negatively impacting resolution rates and surveyed customer satisfaction.

kp.k: Lower-skilled and newer workers gain disproportionately
kp.d: Separate analyses control for tenure when comparing skill groups and for skill when comparing tenure groups. The lowest skill quintile improves resolutions per hour by 34%, while workers with less than one month of tenure improve by 46%. The most skilled workers show no productivity increase, and agents with more than a year of tenure show no effect on resolutions per hour. These findings contrast with earlier computerization literature emphasizing complementarities with higher-skilled labor.
qs: the productivity impact of AI assistance is most pronounced for workers in the lowest skill quintile (leftmost side), who see a .29 log point or 34% increase in resolutions per hour.
Agents with less than 1 month of tenure improve their resolutions per hour by .38 log points or 46% improvement (relative to agents of the same tenure who do not have access to AI assistance).
In contrast, we see no effect for agents with more than a year of tenure.

kp.k: Top performers may experience small quality losses
kp.d: For the highest-skilled workers, the study finds mixed efficiency effects and small statistically significant decreases in resolution rates and customer satisfaction. The authors suggest, rather than establish, that recommendations may distract top performers or encourage faster suggested answers instead of their own better responses. Access to an assistant is therefore not uniformly beneficial across workers or performance dimensions.
qs: Indeed, we find evidence that AI assistance may decrease the quality of conversations by the most skilled agents.
AI recommendations may distract top performers, or lead them to choose the faster option (following suggestions) rather than taking the time to come up with their own responses.

kp.k: AI accelerates progress along the experience curve
kp.d: Workers with two months of tenure and AI access perform as well as or better than workers with more than six months of tenure without access across several outcomes. Workers receiving assistance later also improve rapidly after deployment. The authors distinguish assisted performance from learning: these experience-curve comparisons alone cannot determine whether workers acquire skills or simply follow recommendations.
qs: Across many of the outcomes in Figure 8, agents with two months of tenure and access to AI assistance perform as well as or better than agents with more than six months of tenure who do not have access.
We avoid the term “learning curve” because we cannot distinguish if workers are learning or merely following recommendations.

kp.k: Adherence correlates with gains but is not randomized
kp.d: The detailed adherence analysis reports an average of 38%, with an interquartile range of 23% to 50%; the section introduction separately reports 35%. Productivity gains range from approximately 10% in the lowest initial-adherence quintile to nearly 25% in the highest. Adherence increases over time, including within workers, particularly among initially skeptical and senior workers. The authors explicitly acknowledge selection and selection on gains as alternative explanations for the adherence-productivity relationship.
qs: The average adherence rate is 38%, with an interquartile range of 23% to 50%: agents frequently ignore recommendations.
among agents in the lowest quintile, we still see a 10% gain in productivity, but for agents in the highest quintile, the estimated impact is over twice as high, close to 25%.

We note, however, that this relationship could also be driven by other factors: selection (agents who choose to adhere are more productive for other reasons); or selection on gains (agents who follow recommendations are those with the greatest returns).

kp.k: Outage evidence suggests durable learning from AI assistance
kp.d: During software outages, previously exposed workers continue to handle chats faster than before adoption, with stronger improvements after longer exposure and among workers with high initial adherence. Low-adherence workers show no such improvement. The authors interpret this as suggestive evidence of durable skill acquisition and a potential supplement to brief managerial coaching, while warning that outage estimates are noisy and outages are rare and not necessarily random.
qs: Because AI outages are rare and not necessarily random, this may reflect differences in the types of chats that are seen during outage periods than during non-outage periods.
Yet, if an outage occurs after three months of exposure to AI recommendations, workers handle the chat faster—even though they are not receiving direct AI assistance.
Together, these results suggest that generative AI tools can help workers develop durable skills.

kp.k: Communication changes support a best-practice diffusion mechanism
kp.d: Text-embedding analysis finds that communication changes immediately after AI deployment, more strongly for lower-skilled workers. Similarity between lower- and higher-skilled workers increases from approximately 0.55 to 0.61. The authors interpret these patterns as suggestive evidence that models disseminate higher performers' practices, including tacit knowledge, rather than merely enabling faster typing. This remains a proposed mechanism supported by converging evidence, not a separately identified causal channel.
qs: This drop in similarity is broadly inconsistent with the idea that AI assistance merely leads workers to type the same things but faster.
Together, the patterns in Figures 13 and 14 suggest that low-skill workers are converging toward high-skill workers, rather than the opposite.
This finding is consistent with AI models disseminating the behaviors of high-skilled workers to lower-skilled workers.

kp.k: Customer sentiment improves and escalation requests decline
kp.d: Model-based sentiment analysis estimates a 0.18-point improvement in customer sentiment, approximately half a standard deviation, with immediate and persistent effects. Customer requests to speak to managers decline almost 25% relative to a baseline around 6%. These outcomes concern expressed sentiment and requests, not measured actual escalations or an improvement in average surveyed net promoter scores. Less-skilled and less-experienced agents generally benefit most.
qs: access to AI improves the mean customer sentiments (averaged over an agent-month) by 0.18 points, equivalent to half of a standard deviation.
Following the introduction of AI assistance, we see a gradual decline in requests for escalation.
Relative to a baseline rate of approximately 6 percentage points, these coefficients suggest that AI assistance generates an almost 25% decline in customer requests to speak to a manager.

kp.k: Retention improves, but causal confidence is weaker
kp.d: AI access is associated with approximately 10 percentage points lower attrition among agents with less than six months of experience, a 40% decrease relative to their 25% baseline. Attrition decreases significantly across skill groups without a systematic skill gradient. The authors caution that this analysis cannot include agent fixed effects and may overstate effects if access was preferentially given to workers expected to remain.
qs: The magnitude of this coefficient, around 10 percentage points, translates into a 40% decrease relative to a baseline attrition rate in this group of 25%.
Our results may overstate the impact of AI access on attrition if, for example, access to the AI tool is more likely to be given to agents whom the firm believes are more likely to stay.

kp.k: Employment and wage consequences remain unresolved
kp.d: The study does not measure aggregate employment, wages, hiring composition or long-run job redesign. The authors describe competing possibilities: firms might hire more novices, de-skill jobs or develop replacement systems; higher productivity could reduce labor demand if customer-support demand is inelastic, while better support could expand demand and responsibilities. These are conditional scenarios, not demonstrated displacement or employment-growth findings.
qs: We emphasize, however, that our paper is not designed to shed light on the aggregate employment or wage effects of generative AI tools.
Unfortunately, our data do not allow us to observe changes in wages, overall labor demand, or the skill composition of workers hired for the job.
It is unclear, for example, whether improvements in customer service productivity will lead to more or less demand for customer service workers.

kp.k: Training-data contributions create compensation and incentive questions
kp.d: The authors argue that worker productivity includes providing examples that improve models and other workers' performance. Top performers supplied many training examples but gained comparatively little themselves; relative-performance bonuses could even reduce their pay as colleagues improve. This is presented as a potential compensation and long-term incentive problem, not an observed wage effect or a specified compensation policy.
qs: Top workers are generally not paid for their contributions to the training data that AI systems use to capture and disseminate their skills.
Under our data firm’s current pay practices, these workers may even see a reduction in their pay because bonuses are calculated relative to other agents’ performance.
Our results therefore raise questions about how workers, particularly top performers, should be compensated for the data that they provide to AI systems.

kp.k: Generalization depends on workflow and changing knowledge
kp.d: The authors caution that results from a relatively stable product and technical-support environment may not generalize to other firms or production processes. In rapidly changing settings, AI could either synthesize evolving best practices or impede learning by recommending outdated ones. They also identify misleading output, workers' ability to recognize inappropriate advice, and complementary organizational investment as constraints on real-world effectiveness.
qs: the effects we find may not generalize across all firms and production processes (Eloundou et al., 2023).
For example, our setting has a relatively stable product and a set of technical support questions.
they may be better able to synthesize changing best practices, or they may actually impede learning by promoting outdated practices observed in historical training data.
Promising technologies may have more limited effects in practice due to the need for complementary organizational investments, skill development, or business process redesign.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Brynjolfsson, Li and Raymond report that AI assistance increases customer-support productivity, with disproportionately large gains for less-skilled and less-experienced agents, and suggest that it spreads best practices and supports learning.
pts.d: This is a cross-domain study of customer support, not a study of legal services. The authors report an average productivity increase of approximately 14%, measured by successfully resolved issues per hour. Their preferred specification estimates 0.30 additional resolutions per hour, or 13.8%. The lowest pre-treatment skill quintile gains 34%; separately, agents with less than one month of tenure gain 46%. The most skilled workers show no productivity increase, and the most experienced show little or none. Some measures of conversation quality decline for the highest-skilled and most-experienced agents. Average chat duration falls approximately 9%, chats handled per hour rise approximately 14%, resolution rates increase modestly, and surveyed customer satisfaction does not materially change overall. The authors also report improved customer sentiment, almost 25% fewer requests to speak to a manager, and lower attrition, particularly among newer workers. They interpret communication convergence and performance during outages as suggestive evidence of best-practice dissemination and durable learning. They do not conclude that productivity gains necessarily increase or reduce employment: their longer-term scenarios include greater hiring of novices, deskilling, substitution, or expanded customer-support responsibilities.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The principal evidence is a staggered workplace rollout analysed using difference-in-differences; learning, communication and retention claims rely on additional analyses with explicit qualifications.
pts.d: The supplied body is the April 2023 NBER working paper revised November 2023, notwithstanding the wrapper's 2025 journal citation. It reports approximately three million chats involving 5,179 agents, including approximately 1.2 million post-AI chats involving 1,636 agents. A seven-week randomized pilot involving 50 agents preceded the wider rollout; the principal analysis is not a large randomized trial. Preferred regressions control for agent, calendar time and tenure, with alternative difference-in-differences estimators and event studies used as robustness checks. Resolution rates and customer-satisfaction measures are available only for a subset, limiting the sample for resolutions per hour. Skill heterogeneity uses pre-treatment performance rankings, distinguishing skill from tenure. Outage-period performance and textual embeddings provide suggestive mechanism evidence: outages are rare and not necessarily random, and adherence-productivity associations may reflect selection. Customer sentiment is measured using SiEBERT rather than equated with surveyed satisfaction. Escalation evidence concerns requests, not actual escalations. Attrition analysis cannot include agent fixed effects and may overstate effects if agents expected to stay were preferentially given AI access. Wage and aggregate employment scenarios are not measured findings.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The findings concern near-term, human-in-the-loop assistance in a relatively stable support environment; longer-term and cross-setting outcomes remain conditional.
pts.d: Most adoption occurred between November 2020 and February 2021. Productivity improvements appear in the first month and persist through the observed post-deployment period, with event studies extending approximately five months. Agents with two months of tenure and AI assistance perform as well as or better than unassisted agents with more than six months of tenure. Outage analyses suggest that unaided performance improves after accumulated exposure, rather than proving permanent learning over a long horizon. The system is a copilot: it offers suggested responses and internal-documentation links, while human agents retain responsibility and discretion. It is fine-tuned using the firm's support conversations and performance labels, and withholds suggestions when training data are insufficient. The authors caution that results may not generalize to other firms or rapidly changing environments, where historical recommendations might impede learning. Long-run employment and wage effects depend in part on customer demand; reductions are presented as a possibility if demand is inelastic, not as an observed outcome.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: Effects differ across novice agents, top performers, customers and employers; the authors also identify potential compensation issues for workers whose expertise trains the system.
pts.d: The setting is a Fortune 500 enterprise-software provider serving US small and medium-sized businesses, with support delivered by directly employed and outsourced agents. Approximately 89% of sampled agents are outside the United States, primarily in the Philippines. Novice and lower-performing agents receive the largest productivity benefits and experience faster progression along the experience curve. Among agents with less than six months of experience, AI access is associated with an approximately 10-percentage-point reduction in attrition, or 40% relative to a 25% baseline, subject to the selection caveat. Customers express more positive sentiment and request managers less often. Employers benefit from greater throughput and potentially improved retention, while reduced managerial escalation requests suggest possible workflow implications rather than measured reductions in managerial staffing. Top performers contribute training examples but receive few direct productivity gains; because bonuses depend on relative performance, the authors suggest their pay could fall and raise questions about compensation for training-data contributions. The study does not establish effects on lawyers, legal clients, legal-market staffing or access to justice.
